title: Update in ocular surface squamous neoplasia
clinical_background: OSSN encompasses squamous lesions of the conjunctiva and cornea, ranging from intraepithelial changes to invasive carcinoma. It can resemble common ocular surface conditions and may cause ocular damage and systemic morbidity. These risks make eye protection and early recognition of suspicious lesions important.
study_design: Review of ocular surface squamous neoplasia; no formal review methods are described.
interpretation: Ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN) encompasses lesions ranging from intraepithelial disease to invasive carcinoma. It can resemble common ocular surface conditions, and OSSN may cause ocular damage and systemic morbidity. Histopathological examination of a biopsy remains the diagnostic standard because it establishes the depth of tissue invasion; noninvasive tests can aid characterization. Surgical excision remains the treatment standard, although medical therapies are increasingly used. Recurrence risk varies, with excision margins identified as the most important predictor; invasive carcinoma and mucoepidermoid carcinoma have less favorable prognoses.
clinical_implications: Similarity to benign-appearing ocular surface lesions can make clinical identification difficult and may require further evaluation.

Noninvasive diagnostic methods can support assessment, but impression cytology samples only superficial cells, and in vivo confocal microscopy has produced inconsistent findings that prevent it from reliably replacing biopsy.
Anterior segment optical coherence tomography can help distinguish OSSN from benign ocular surface conditions.
Topical treatment can reach the entire ocular surface, including areas of subclinical disease, and carries a lower risk of conjunctival scarring.

Smaller tumors detected earlier have a better prognosis. Inadequate excision margins increase the tendency toward recurrence, particularly in large lesions (greater than 2 mm), older patients, or lesions involving deep tissue or the cornea.
Late recurrence remains possible even years after treatment.
practice_implications: Promote appropriate eye protection and early ophthalmological diagnosis of suspicious lesions.
Investigate suspicious lesions identified during ophthalmological examination; use biopsy with histopathological analysis when determining tissue invasion.
Consider pterygia, pingueculae, and the other listed ocular surface conditions in the differential diagnosis. Do not treat in vivo confocal microscopy as a reliable replacement for biopsy.
Use surgical excision according to the described Shields “no touch” technique to reduce the potential for tumor seeding.
Topical therapies may be used before surgery to reduce tumor size or after surgery when margins contain tumor.
Reserve MMC often for more recalcitrant cases after failure of other agents because of its adverse effects.
IFN-α2b may be used as primary treatment for small lesions, before surgery for diffuse tumors, or after resection when margins contain tumor.
Reserve enucleation for intraocular invasion and exenteration for periocular invasion.
Monitor patients regularly and permanently, with annual visits, because recurrence can occur years after treatment.
open_questions: The appropriate dose for locally injected IFN-α2b has no established consensus.
The role of anti-VEGF in OSSN remains uncertain because its use as primary treatment or after excision has been described in only a few case reports.
main_conclusion: Earlier detection and smaller tumors are associated with a better prognosis; treatment aims to remove the lesion, prevent recurrence, and preserve vision when possible. Surgical excision remains the treatment standard, although nonsurgical therapies are increasingly used; because recurrence may occur years later, the authors recommend permanent follow-up with annual examinations.
narrative_summary:
This review examines ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN), including its risk factors, clinical features, diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis. It describes ultraviolet B exposure, HPV infection, immunosuppression, and xeroderma pigmentosum as important risk factors. OSSN can resemble benign ocular surface conditions, making recognition and diagnostic assessment important. Histopathological examination after biopsy remains the diagnostic standard and is the only method described as establishing the depth of tissue invasion. OCT-SA can help distinguish OSSN from benign lesions, whereas IVCM should not replace biopsy because its findings are inconsistent.

Treatment seeks to remove the lesion, limit recurrence, and preserve vision where possible. Surgical excision remains the treatment standard. The review also discusses topical mitomycin C (MMC), 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), and interferon-alpha 2b (IFN-α2b), alongside other nonsurgical approaches. Cited evidence for primary topical 5-FU reports efficacy of 85–100% and recurrence ranging from 1.1 to 43%. MMC can cause dry eye, punctal stenosis, persistent epithelial defects, and allergic reactions, and is often reserved for cases unresponsive to other agents. The role of anti-VEGF remains uncertain because the review identifies only a few case reports. Surgical margin status is described as the most important predictor of recurrence. CIN with clear margins generally has a favorable prognosis, but invasive carcinoma and mucoepidermoid carcinoma have less favorable outcomes even after excision with clear margins. The authors recommend permanent monitoring through annual consultations because recurrence can arise years after treatment.

document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: Ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN) covers squamous tumors of the conjunctiva and cornea, including conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), corneal epithelial dysplasia, squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), and mucoepidermoid carcinoma. It can resemble pinguecula, pterygium, conjunctival granulomas, or cysts. Because OSSN can cause substantial ocular injury and systemic morbidity, the article emphasizes public awareness of appropriate eye protection and early assessment of suspicious lesions by ophthalmologists.

document_sections.heading: EPIDEMIOLOGY
document_sections.content: The frequency of OSSN varies worldwide alongside differences in risk factors. In the United States, reported incidence is 0.03–1.9 cases per 100,000 individuals per year; cases predominantly occur in Caucasian men in their sixth and seventh decades. In Africa, reported incidence is higher, at 3 to 3.4 cases per 100,000 individuals per year; affected patients are younger, and no sex predominance is apparent.

document_sections.heading: ETIOLOGY, RISK FACTORS, AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
document_sections.content: OSSN has multiple potential causes, among which immune status may be the most important. Its principal associated risk factors are ultraviolet B (UVB) exposure, human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, immunosuppression, and xeroderma pigmentosum. Greater UVB exposure is linked to the higher OSSN incidence documented near the Equator. The location of most lesions in the sun-exposed interpalpebral fissure and nasal and temporal limbus further supports this association. Nasal limbal epithelial crypts contain basal epithelial stem-cell niches; these cells may give rise to OSSN after alteration, with subsequent surface spread and later penetration of the basement membrane. UVB can damage DNA by generating pyrimidine dimers and mutations involving the p53 tumor suppressor gene, allowing cells with damaged DNA to pass a cell-cycle checkpoint. HPV can cause intraepithelial injury that progresses to squamous neoplasia; subtypes 16 and 18 are specifically associated with ocular-surface neoplastic lesions. UV radiation has also been described as producing local and systemic photoimmunosuppression and potentially reactivating latent viruses such as HPV. Immunodeficient people, particularly those with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), have an approximately 10 times greater risk of OSSN and frequently experience poorer outcomes after treatment. Impaired DNA repair, as seen in xeroderma pigmentosum, is another etiological factor. Further risk factors include older age, male sex, lightly pigmented hair and eyes, xerophthalmia, ocular-surface trauma, smoking, and prolonged exposure to petroleum products. Vitamin A deficiency compromises ocular-surface integrity, producing microabrasions that permit HPV entry into the basement membrane and conjunctival epithelial cells and thereby initiate local cellular changes.

document_sections.heading: GENERAL PATHOLOGY AND HISTOPATHOLOGY
document_sections.content: The classification described for OSSN includes dysplastic and carcinomatous ocular-surface lesions. Its benign category includes pseudotheliomatous hyperplasia, benign hereditary intraepithelial dyskeratosis, and papillomas. Preinvasive OSSN, termed intraepithelial neoplasias (CIN), comprises CIN I, with mild dysplasia limited to the lower third of conjunctival epithelium; CIN II, with moderate dysplasia reaching the middle third; and CIN III, with severe dysplasia reaching the upper third. Dysplasia spanning the full epithelial thickness is termed carcinoma in situ (CIS). Invasive OSSN crosses the epithelial basement membrane and extends into conjunctival stroma and neighboring structures. This category includes SCC and mucoepidermoid carcinoma; the latter is more aggressive and more prone to recurrence than SCC.

document_sections.heading: HISTORY
document_sections.content: Many people with OSSN have no symptoms, and suspicion often arises during a routine ophthalmological examination. Others notice an elevated conjunctival mass, sometimes with irritation, itching, or ocular redness.

document_sections.heading: CLINICAL PRESENTATION
document_sections.content: OSSN typically appears as a raised, nodular lesion in the interpalpebral area. Its color can range from grayish white to red, its edges may be irregular, and visible vessels often accompany it. Benign OSSN usually has a papillomatous appearance. CIN may appear leukoplastic, gelatinous, or both: leukoplastic lesions show surface hyperkeratinization, whereas gelatinous lesions tend to be reddish and sharply demarcated and may be nodular or diffuse. Corneal involvement arising from abnormal epithelial cells spreading from the limbus appears avascular, translucent, opalescent, and groundglass-like, generally with clear borders. Conjunctival SCC can resemble CIN, but its conjunctival lesion tends to be more elevated, plaque-shaped, and less mobile. Feeding vessels in such lesions suggest disruption and invasion of the epithelial basement membrane. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is a more aggressive, recurrent variant that clinically resembles SCC and can occur at any ocular-surface location.

document_sections.heading: DIAGNOSIS
document_sections.content: OSSN diagnosis generally combines clinical information, ophthalmological examination, gross lesion features, noninvasive ancillary tests, and histopathology. Recognizing a suspicious lesion on eye examination is the essential starting point for investigation. Histopathological examination after biopsy remains the diagnostic gold standard despite its invasiveness, because it alone can establish how deeply the lesion has invaded tissue. Interest in less invasive assessment has grown, and vital dyes, cytology, confocal microscopy, and anterior segment optical coherence tomography (OCT-SA) have been used to characterize lesions. Rose bengal, methylene blue, and toluidine blue can assist diagnosis. Rose bengal identifies degenerated epithelial cells, and methylene blue helps detect malignant lesions, but neither is specific to OSSN. Toluidine blue stains cells with high mitotic activity and accumulates between cells, particularly where adhesion is limited; its reported sensitivity for diagnosing OSSN is 92%, while specificity is 31%. Cytology may be exfoliative or performed by impression. Impression cytology collects surface cells by applying cellulose acetate filter paper to the lesion. It is minimally invasive and can achieve up to 80% agreement with histopathological samples, but samples only superficial cells and requires interpretation by an experienced cytologist. Studies of in vivo confocal microscopy (IVCM) in OSSN have produced differing results, with considerable overlap between benign and malignant findings. IVCM may sometimes supplement histology, but inconsistent results mean it should not replace biopsy. Anterior Segment Optical Coherence Tomography provides high-resolution views of superficial ocular layers without direct contact or an invasive procedure. OSSN-associated features include an abrupt boundary between normal and abnormal epithelium, abnormal epithelial thickening, and tumor-region hyper-reflectivity. OCT-SA is described as effective for distinguishing OSSN from benign disorders and identifying other tumors, aiding diagnosis and management of ocular-surface disease.

document_sections.heading: DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
document_sections.content: Pterygia and pingueculae are important OSSN differentials because they share risk factors and may occur as synchronous lesions. Other possible alternatives include amelanotic melanoma, corneal pannus, nodular corneal degeneration, pyogenic granuloma, sebaceous cell carcinoma, actinic keratosis, conjunctival cysts, and Bitot’s spots. Overlapping clinical appearances can make differentiation difficult, so additional assessment may be needed to establish the diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: TREATMENT
document_sections.content: Treatment seeks to remove OSSN, prevent recurrence, and preserve sight when feasible. Earlier identification and smaller tumors are associated with better prognosis. Surgical excision remains the treatment gold standard, although medical approaches that avoid surgery have become more common. Conjunctival excision uses Shields “no touch” technique to reduce potential tumor seeding, with wide tumor-free margins and cryotherapy to the remaining conjunctiva using “double freeze, slow thaw.” Cryotherapy is avoided at the limbus to prevent injury to limbal stem cells. Recommended contact time is 3 s in one single application. Corneal disease is removed by alcohol keratoepitheliectomy, and scleral involvement is treated with partial lamellar sclerotomy. A residual conjunctival defect can be closed primarily if it is less than 3 clock hours; for defects of more than 3 clock hours, conjunctival autografts or amniotic membrane grafts may be used. An incisional biopsy for extensive lesions or an excisional biopsy permits histopathological diagnosis. Enucleation is reserved for intraocular invasion and exenteration for periocular invasion. Nonsurgical options comprise topical chemotherapy with mitomycin C (MMC) or 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), injected or topical interferon alpha-2b immunotherapy, topical cidofovir, anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) treatment, and photodynamic therapy (PDT). Topical treatment reaches the entire ocular surface, including subclinical disease, and carries a lower risk of conjunctival scarring. It can also serve as preoperative chemoreduction or as postoperative adjunctive treatment for tumor-positive margins. MMC is an alkylating antineoplastic agent that induces apoptosis and inhibits fibroblast migration, affecting proliferating and non-proliferating cells. Regimens reported as effective are 1 drop of MMC 0.02% three times daily for two 1-week courses and 1 drop of MMC 0.04% four times daily for two 1-week courses. Its adverse effects include dry eye, punctal stenosis, persistent epithelial defects, and allergic reactions; consequently, MMC is often reserved for refractory cases after other agents have failed. 5-FU is a pyrimidine analog that inhibits DNA formation by blocking thymidine synthase and acts during the S phase. Reported topical schedules use a 1% 5-FU formulation four times daily for four weeks, or for 1 week followed by a drug holiday of 3 weeks. Reported efficacy with primary treatment is 85–100%, and recurrence ranges from 1.1 to 43%. Topical 5-FU mainly causes pain and redness at the instillation site, with fewer adverse effects than MMC. It is used alongside topical corticosteroids and preservative-free artificial tears to lessen symptoms. Interferon-alpha 2b (IFN-α2b) is an OSSN immunotherapy. Interferons are naturally occurring glycoproteins with antimicrobial and antiviral activity; their antitumor effects involve antiproliferative, antiangiogenic, and cytotoxic actions and a potential capacity to induce host antitumor immunosurveillance. IFN-α2b may be primary treatment for small lesions, neoadjuvant treatment to facilitate resection of diffuse tumors, or adjunctive treatment after resection with tumor-positive margins. It may be given as topical drops or perilesional subconjunctival injections. The topical schedule is 1 million IU/mL, one drop four times per day without interruption until one or two more months after clinical resolution. There is no consensus on the injected local dose; the described subconjunctival schedule is 3 million IU/0.5 mL weekly until OSSN resolves, generally requiring 4 or 5 injections. Injections cause more adverse effects than drops, including flu-like symptoms. Cidofovir acts against double-stranded DNA viruses, including HPV; topical cidofovir at 2.5 mg/mL has shown good efficacy as secondary treatment for multi-refractory OSSN. Anti-VEGF agents are monoclonal antibodies that impede blood-vessel growth by blocking VEGF interaction with its receptor. Only a few case reports describe their use as primary OSSN treatment or after excision, leaving their role uncertain.

document_sections.heading: PROGNOSIS
document_sections.content: OSSN recurrence after treatment varies, and the surgical excision margin is identified as the most important predictor. CIN with clear margins generally has a favorable prognosis and low local-recurrence rates. Inadequate margins increase the tendency to recur, particularly with large lesions (greater than 2 mm), older patients, or deep-tissue or corneal involvement; recurrence reaches up to one-third of cases. Invasive carcinoma and mucoepidermoid carcinoma have poorer prognoses and higher local-recurrence rates even after surgery with clear margins. Because recurrence can arise years after treatment, regular permanent surveillance with annual consultations is recommended.
